lessons.title: Hash tables: the map ADT and hash functions
lessons.summary: You will be able to state what insert, search and delete must do, compare the four implementations on slide 3 of Lecture 2 by their search and insert costs, and explain why hashing reaches O(1) on average. Covers the three properties of a good hash function — deterministic, uniform, fast — and the load factor alpha = n / m. Prevents claiming O(1) in the worst case: with every key landing in one bucket, search is O(n).

payload.markdown:
Slide 3 of Lecture 2 lists the dictionary (map) ADT as three operations: `insert(key, value)`, `search(key)`, `delete(key)`. That is the whole contract. A map is not a list with nicer syntax — it is a promise that given a key you can get its value back, and the only question that matters on the exam is what each implementation charges you for that promise.

Slide 3 gives the price list:

| Implementation | Search | Insert |
|---|---|---|
| Unsorted array | O(n) | O(1) |
| Sorted array | O(log n) | O(n) |
| Balanced binary search tree | O(log n) | O(log n) |
| Hash table | O(1) average | O(1) average |

Read the table as a trade, not a ranking. An unsorted array inserts in O(1) because you drop the pair at the end and walk away; search is O(n) because nothing about the position tells you where the key is. A sorted array buys O(log n) search with binary search and pays O(n) on insert, because a new key in the middle shifts everything after it. The balanced BST is the only one that refuses to be bad at either — O(log n) both ways — and that is why it costs you pointer bookkeeping and rotations.

The hash table is the odd one out because it is the only row with the word *average*. Nothing about a hash table makes search O(1) by construction. It makes search O(1) **when the keys are spread**, and the rest of this lesson is about what "spread" means and what happens when it fails.

The mechanism is two steps. A hash function turns the key into a bucket index. The table stores the entry in that bucket. Search recomputes the same index and looks only there. If the buckets hold roughly one entry each, that lookup touches one entry and the cost is constant. If every key lands in bucket 0, the lookup walks a list of n entries and the cost is O(n) — the same as the unsorted array, with extra arithmetic on top.

Slide 5 names the three properties a hash function must have: **deterministic** (the same key always gives the same index), **uniform** (keys spread evenly over the buckets), and **fast to compute, using the whole key**. Deterministic is not a nice-to-have. If `h("Ada")` returns 3 on insert and 5 on search, the entry is unreachable and the map is broken, not slow.

Slide 5 also gives the division method, `h(k) = k mod m`, with the warning to choose m prime and not close to a power of 2. The reason is uniformity. With m = 16, `k mod 16` keeps only the low 4 bits of k, so any set of keys that agrees in those bits — student IDs ending in 00, timestamps on a 16 ms tick — piles into one bucket. A prime m mixes all the bits of k into the index instead.

The last quantity is the **load factor** α = n / m, where n is the number of entries and m is the number of buckets. Slide 13 uses it to split the two collision strategies: separate chaining keeps entries in lists outside the array and lets α exceed 1, while open addressing keeps everything inside the array and must stay below 1. Both give O(1) average and O(n) worst case — slide 13 states both columns explicitly.

payload.markdown:
A hash table is a cloakroom with m numbered hooks. The hash function is the rule the attendant uses to decide which hook your coat goes on: `h(k) = k mod m`. Hand over a coat and the attendant computes the hook, hangs the coat, and writes nothing down. Come back with the same ticket and the attendant recomputes the same hook and finds your coat immediately — that is the O(1) average.

When two coats hash to the same hook, the attendant hangs the second coat on the same hook (chaining, slide 9: 50, 85 and 92 all hang on hook 1) or walks along the rail to the next free hook (open addressing, slide 11: 49 wants hook 9, finds it taken, takes hook 0). Either way you now have to look at more than one coat.

If every coat hashes to hook 1, the attendant stands at hook 1 and lifts coats one at a time until yours appears. That is O(n), and no amount of arithmetic changes it.
payload.breaks_down_when: The cloakroom has a physical rail, so a full hook is obvious and the attendant can see the whole row at a glance. A hash table has no such view: open addressing can only follow the probe sequence one slot at a time, which is why deleting an entry needs a tombstone (slide 13) rather than simply removing the coat — pulling a coat off the rail would break the chain of slots that later searches must walk through.

blocks.title: Insert 44, 57, 91, 18, 83 into m = 7 with h(k) = k mod 7, then search for 18

payload.title: Insert 44, 57, 91, 18, 83 into m = 7 with h(k) = k mod 7, then search for 18
payload.markdown:
Chaining, m = 7, new entries go to the end of the chain (slide 9's convention).

| Key | k mod 7 | Bucket after insert |
|---|---|---|
| 44 | 44 − 42 = 2 | 2: 44 |
| 57 | 57 − 56 = 1 | 1: 57 |
| 91 | 91 − 91 = 0 | 0: 91 |
| 18 | 18 − 14 = 4 | 4: 18 |
| 83 | 83 − 77 = 6 | 6: 83 |

Every key landed in its own bucket, so α = 5/7 ≈ 0.71 and every search costs one comparison.

Now add 64 and 36, both of which collide:

| Key | k mod 7 | Bucket after insert |
|---|---|---|
| 64 | 64 − 63 = 1 | 1: 57 → 64 |
| 36 | 36 − 35 = 1 | 1: 57 → 64 → 36 |

`search(18)`: compute 18 mod 7 = 4, look at bucket 4, compare 18 with 18, return the value. **1 comparison.**

`search(36)`: compute 36 mod 7 = 1, look at bucket 1, compare 36 with 57 (no), compare 36 with 64 (no), compare 36 with 36 (yes). **3 comparisons.**

`search(50)`: compute 50 mod 7 = 1, walk the whole chain 57, 64, 36 and find nothing. **3 comparisons and a failed search** — the worst case for a lookup is a miss, because you must exhaust the chain to be sure.

With n = 7 and m = 7, α = 1.0. The average chain length is 1, but the longest chain is 3, and that is the number the exam will ask you to count.

payload.intro: Trace a linear-probing insertion the way you will on paper, with slide 11's example: insert 89, 18, 49, 58, 69 into m = 10 with h(k) = k mod 10. Probe h(k), then h(k)+1, h(k)+2, wrapping past 9 back to 0, and count every slot you examine, the first one included.

steps.title: Write the empty table and the rule
steps.detail_markdown: Draw slots 0 to 9. Write the rule at the top: `h(k) = k mod 10`, probe forward, wrap at 9 back to 0. Every probe is one slot examined, including the first.

steps.title: Insert 89 and 18
steps.detail_markdown: 89 mod 10 = 9: slot 9 is empty, so place 89 there. 18 mod 10 = 8: slot 8 is empty, so place 18 there. **1 probe each.**

steps.title: Insert 49: the first collision
steps.detail_markdown: 49 mod 10 = 9. Slot 9 holds 89, so probe on: wrap to slot 0, which is empty. Place 49 at slot 0. **2 probes** (slots 9, 0).
steps.warning: Count the home slot too. 49 has one collision but needs 2 probes; slide 11 writes it as '49 → 9 taken, try 0: 2 probes'.

steps.title: Insert 58: walk the run
steps.detail_markdown: 58 mod 10 = 8. Slots 8 (18), 9 (89) and 0 (49) are taken, so the next try is slot 1, which is empty. Place 58 at slot 1. **4 probes** (slots 8, 9, 0, 1).

steps.title: Insert 69: the run grows again
steps.detail_markdown: 69 mod 10 = 9. Slots 9 (89), 0 (49) and 1 (58) are taken, so try slot 2: empty. Place 69 at slot 2. **4 probes** (slots 9, 0, 1, 2).
steps.warning: This is primary clustering: the occupied run 8, 9, 0, 1 caught 69 and grew to 8, 9, 0, 1, 2. Any key that hashes into a run lands at its end and makes it longer.

steps.title: Write the final table
steps.detail_markdown: Final table: 0 → 49, 1 → 58, 2 → 69, 3 to 7 empty, 8 → 18, 9 → 89, exactly as on slide 11. Probes per insert: 1, 1, 2, 4, 4. Load factor α = 5/10 = 0.5.

payload.belief: A hash table search is O(1), so it is always at least as fast as a balanced BST.
payload.why_it_seems_right: Slide 3 prints "Hash table — Search: O(1) average" right next to "Balanced binary search tree — Search: O(log n)", and the average is the case you see in every example you have traced. payload.what_is_true: Slide 13 lists the worst case for both chaining and open addressing as O(n), and the average only holds when the hash function is uniform and α is kept in check. If every key hashes to the same bucket, search walks all n entries — strictly worse than a balanced BST's guaranteed O(log n), because you also paid the hash computation. The balanced BST's O(log n) is a worst-case bound; the hash table's O(1) is an average that depends on a property of your hash function, not on the data structure alone. On an exam, "O(1)" written without "average" for a hash table is a lost mark.

lessons.title: Binary search trees: search, insert and delete
lessons.summary: You will be able to run search and insert down a tree and delete any node, redrawing the tree after each change. Covers the vocabulary from slide 3 of Lecture 3 (root, leaf, subtree, depth, height), the iterative search loop, in-order traversal giving sorted output, and the three deletion cases including the in-order successor for a node with two children. Prevents cutting out a two-child node in a way that breaks the sorted order.

payload.markdown:
A BST is a binary tree with one extra rule: for every node, everything in its left subtree is smaller and everything in its right subtree is bigger. That single rule is what lets you search in O(h) instead of scanning every node.

Slide 3 of Lecture 3 fixes the vocabulary you will be marked on:

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Root | the top node; no parent |
| Leaf | a node with no children |
| Subtree | a node plus all its descendants |
| Depth of a node | number of edges from the root |
| Height of a tree | number of edges on the longest root-to-leaf path |
| Binary tree | every node has at most two children |

Slide 5 gives the search loop. It is iterative, not recursive:

```javascript
function search(node, key) {
  while (node !== null && key !== node.key)
    node = key < node.key ? node.left : node.right;
  return node; // null when the key is absent
}
```

Each comparison sends you exactly one level down, so the cost is O(h). Insert is the same walk with one extra move: search for the key, and when the walk falls off the tree, attach a new leaf there. Delete is the hard one, and it has three cases — slide 7 lists them. A leaf just goes. A node with one child is replaced by that child. A node with two children is replaced by its in-order successor, the smallest key in its right subtree, and then that successor is deleted from where it sat.

Why the successor and not just any node? Because in-order traversal of a BST visits keys in sorted order. Slide 6 shows it on the example tree: in-order gives 20 30 40 50 60 70 80, pre-order gives 50 30 20 40 70 60 80, post-order gives 20 40 30 60 80 70 50. The successor is the next key in that sorted list, so putting it where the deleted node was keeps the sorted order intact.

lessons.title: Binary heaps: priority queue operations
lessons.summary: You will be able to insert into a heap, extract the minimum, and write out the array that holds the tree after every swap. Covers the shape property and heap property from slide 4 of Lecture 4, the parent index floor((i − 1) / 2), sift-up, sift-down, find-min in O(1) and insert and extract-min in O(log n). Prevents inserting anywhere except the end and breaking the complete tree.

payload.markdown:
Slide 3 of Lecture 4 lists what a priority queue must do: every element carries a priority, and the highest-priority element leaves first. The operations are `insert`, `peek` (find-min or find-max), and `extract-min` or `extract-max`. The applications on that slide are CPU and job scheduling, Dijkstra's shortest paths and Prim's minimum spanning tree, event-driven simulation, heapsort, and finding the k largest items in a stream.

A binary heap is the structure that makes those operations cheap. Slide 4 gives the two properties that define it, and both must hold at once:

- **Shape property** — a complete binary tree: every level is full except possibly the last, and the last fills from the left.
- **Heap property** — in a min-heap every parent is ≤ its children, so the minimum sits at the root. (A max-heap reverses the comparison.)

A heap is not sorted. Siblings have no order between them. In the array `[1, 3, 6, 5, 9, 8]`, the children of the root are 3 and 6, and 5, 9, 8 sit under them in an order that carries no meaning.

The shape property is what lets you drop pointers entirely. Slide 5 stores the nodes level by level in an array with index 0 as the root, and for the node at index `i`:

```
left child:  2i + 1
right child: 2i + 2
parent:      Math.floor((i - 1) / 2)
```

That array `[1, 3, 6, 5, 9, 8]` is the tree

```
      1
     / \
    3   6
   / \ /
  5  9 8
```

Check it against the formulas. Index 1 holds 3; its children are indices 3 and 4, holding 5 and 9. Index 2 holds 6; its left child is index 5, holding 8, and its right child would be index 6, which does not exist. Index 5's parent is `Math.floor((5 - 1) / 2) = 2`, holding 6. Every parent is ≤ its children, and the tree is complete, so this is a valid min-heap.

Because the shape is fixed, only two operations can ever disturb the heap, and each has exactly one repair: `insert` adds at the end and sifts **up**; `extract-min` moves the last leaf to the root and sifts **down**. Slide 12 prices them: find-min is O(1), insert and extract-min are O(log n), and building a heap from n items is O(n).

payload.intro: Slide 7 of Lecture 4 traces one insert into the heap `[1, 3, 6, 5, 9, 8]`. Here is the same procedure run on a different heap, with every array written out. Keep the array on paper and move the index with your finger — the exam marks the array after each swap, not just the final one.

steps.title: Write the starting heap and confirm it is valid
steps.detail_markdown: Start from `[4, 7, 9, 12, 8, 10]`. Check the shape: indices 0–5 exist, so the tree has a root, two children, and three leaves at indices 3, 4, 5 — level 0 full, level 1 full, level 2 filling from the left. Check the heap property: index 1 holds 7 with children at 3 (12) and 4 (8), and 7 ≤ 12 and 7 ≤ 8. Index 2 holds 9 with left child at 5 (10), and 9 ≤ 10. Valid min-heap.
steps.check: You can name the parent of index 4 as `Math.floor((4 - 1) / 2) = 1` without hesitating.

steps.title: Append the new key at the end
steps.detail_markdown: Insert 5. The new key goes at index 6 — the next free slot, which keeps the tree complete. Array becomes `[4, 7, 9, 12, 8, 10, 5]`. Do not compare-and-place it anywhere else; the shape property forces the position.
steps.warning: Writing 5 next to the 4 at the root, or anywhere except the end, breaks the complete-tree shape. The array would no longer be a heap no matter how the comparisons come out.
steps.check: Array length is 7, and the new key is at index 6.

steps.title: Find the parent of the new key
steps.detail_markdown: `i = 6`, so `p = Math.floor((6 - 1) / 2) = Math.floor(2.5) = 2`. Index 2 holds 9. Compare: is `heap[2] <= heap[6]`? 9 ≤ 5 is false, so the heap property is violated and you must swap.
steps.check: You computed 2, not 3 — integer division truncates, it does not round.

steps.title: Swap with the parent and move up
steps.detail_markdown: Swap indices 2 and 6: `[4, 7, 5, 12, 8, 10, 9]`. The 5 is now at index 2. Set `i = 2` and repeat.
steps.check: The 9 that was at index 2 now sits at index 6, the last slot.

steps.title: Repeat at the new index
steps.detail_markdown: `i = 2`, so `p = Math.floor((2 - 1) / 2) = 0`. Index 0 holds 4. Compare: 4 ≤ 5 is true. The heap property holds, so break out of the loop. No swap.
steps.check: You stopped. The loop condition `i > 0` is still true, but `heap[p] <= heap[i]` (4 ≤ 5) is now true, and that `break` is the exit.

steps.title: Write the final array and verify
steps.detail_markdown: Final array: `[4, 7, 5, 12, 8, 10, 9]`. Verify every parent: index 0 (4) ≤ 7 and 5; index 1 (7) ≤ 12 and 8; index 2 (5) ≤ 10 and 9. Shape is still complete. One swap, one level: sift-up makes at most one swap per level, so the cost is bounded by the height, O(log n).
steps.check: The array has the same 7 keys you started with plus the 5, and every parent-child pair passes the comparison.

payload.title: Before you hand in a heap trace

items.text: Every intermediate array has the same length as the number of keys inserted so far.
items.why: A dropped or duplicated key is the fastest way to lose every mark after it.

items.text: Each new key was written at the last index, `heap.length - 1`, before any comparison.
items.why: Inserting anywhere else breaks the complete-tree shape, which no amount of swapping repairs.

items.text: Every parent index is `Math.floor((i - 1) / 2)`, computed with truncation.
items.why: Rounding instead of truncating sends you to the wrong parent on even indices: for i = 6, (6 − 1) / 2 = 2.5 must become 2, not 3.

items.text: Each swap is shown as a separate array, not summarised as one final array.
items.why: The marks are for the swaps; a single final array cannot show that you did them.

items.text: Sift-up stopped at the first index where the parent is ≤ the key, not at the root by default.
items.why: Over-swapping past the stopping point produces an array that is not the algorithm's output.

items.text: For extract-min, the last leaf was moved to index 0 before any comparison, and the old root was recorded as the returned minimum.
items.why: Sifting down the old root instead of the last leaf gives a different, wrong array.

items.text: At each sift-down step you compared the node with BOTH children and swapped with the smaller one.
items.why: Swapping with the larger child puts a bigger value above a smaller one and violates the heap property.

items.text: The final array passes the parent check at every index: `heap[Math.floor((i-1)/2)] <= heap[i]` for all i > 0.
items.why: This is the only self-check that catches a swap you forgot to write down.

payload.title: One extract-min, swap by swap
payload.markdown:
Take the heap `[4, 7, 5, 12, 8, 10, 9]` from the walkthrough and run `extractMin` on it, following slide 8.

**Record the minimum.** `min = heap[0] = 4`. This is what the function returns; it is not part of the array any more.

**Remove the last leaf.** `last = heap.pop()` removes 9, leaving `[4, 7, 5, 12, 8, 10]`. The array is one shorter.

**Move the last leaf to the root.** `heap[0] = 9`, giving `[9, 7, 5, 12, 8, 10]`. The shape is complete again, but the root is 9 and its children are 7 and 5 — the heap property is broken.

**Sift down from i = 0.**

| i | node | left child | right child | smallest of the three | action | array |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 9 | index 1 = 7 | index 2 = 5 | 5 at index 2 | swap 0 and 2 | `[5, 7, 9, 12, 8, 10]` |
| 2 | 9 | index 5 = 10 | index 6 — does not exist | 9 | stop | `[5, 7, 9, 12, 8, 10]` |

At `i = 2` the left child is 10 and 9 < 10, so the node is already the smallest of the three and the loop breaks.

**Result.** `extractMin` returns 4, and the heap is `[5, 7, 9, 12, 8, 10]`. Verify it: index 0 (5) ≤ 7 and 9; index 1 (7) ≤ 12 and 8; index 2 (9) ≤ 10. One swap, one level down — the cost is the height, O(log n).

Note what did *not* happen: the 9 did not travel to the bottom of the tree, and the array did not come back sorted. A heap only promises the root is the minimum.

cites.excerpt: Extract-min: sift-down function extractMin(heap) { const min = heap[0]; const last = heap.pop(); if (heap.length > 0) { heap[0] = last; // move the last leaf to the root let i = 0; while (true) { const l = 2 * i + 1, r = l + 1; let s = i; // index of the smallest of i, l, r if (l < heap.length && heap[l] < heap[s]) s = l; if (r < heap.length && heap[r] < heap[s]) s = r; if (s === i) break; [heap[s], heap[i]] = [heap[i], heap[s]]; i = s; } } return min; }
